Source recommendation: Choose a topic that allows students to investigate and use mathematics, rather than merely describe, research or reproduce existing mathematics.
Encourage students to begin with a genuine question, curiosity, observation or problem that they want to investigate.
Select topics connected to students' interests, experiences or other subjects where this creates opportunities for authentic mathematical investigation.
Ensure the mathematical investigation, not the surrounding real-world context, remains the central focus.
Choose a focused, realistic and achievable aim rather than one that is vague, overly broad or involves several disconnected objectives.
Check that the topic offers sufficient mathematical depth for the student's course while remaining understandable and manageable.
Ensure that the student can access the necessary data, measurements, mathematical tools or other resources before committing to an investigation.
Prefer mathematics students understand well to advanced mathematics that they cannot adequately explain.
Do not assume that using mathematics beyond the syllabus automatically increases marks.
Avoid topics that consist largely of reproducing standard textbook solutions, established proofs, published derivations or well-known demonstrations.

Be particularly cautious with heavily recycled topics, including the golden ratio, Fibonacci numbers, Monty Hall, the birthday paradox, SIR models and Fourier methods. These are not automatically prohibited, but simply reproducing established work provides little opportunity for mathematical ownership.
Consider a broader range of mathematical approaches instead of defaulting to correlation, linear regression and routine statistical tests.
AI SL: Encourage exploration of modelling, optimization, geometry, trigonometry, probability, networks, Voronoi diagrams, financial mathematics and appropriate applications of calculus.
AA SL / AA HL: Do not overlook appropriate investigations involving pure mathematics, proof, algebra, trigonometry, vectors, sequences and series.
Ensure interdisciplinary explorations remain mathematical investigations rather than exercises in applying formulae from physics, economics or another subject.
Check that explorations involving coding, simulations or computer science demonstrate genuine mathematical reasoning rather than being dominated by programming.
Consider whether the topic provides opportunities for students to make mathematical decisions, test ideas, compare methods and reflect critically.
Recognise that some familiar problems can become worthwhile explorations when students meaningfully adapt, extend or personalise the mathematics.
Avoid committing students to a final mathematical procedure before the data or initial analysis has justified that approach.
Allow students to refine the direction of their investigation as their knowledge develops and their mathematical results emerge.

AA HL: Mathematics from the SL portion of the syllabus can be commensurate with the HL course. However, using only SL mathematics requires a depth or sophistication of application beyond ordinary SL expectations to access the highest Criterion E levels.
State the investigation's aim clearly and early in the introduction.
Ensure that the title, aim and any research question or hypothesis are consistent rather than subtly describing different investigations.
Keep the introduction focused on the essential context, motivation and purpose of the investigation.
Avoid lengthy personal rationales, historical background, definitions or general information that do not contribute to the mathematical investigation.
Use a coherent progression from the introduction through the mathematical exploration to the conclusion.
Avoid imposing the structure of an Extended Essay, scientific report or the former Mathematical Studies project on the exploration.
Do not add unnecessary methodology, literature review, contents, strengths-and-weaknesses or planning sections.
Avoid an introductory plan that commits the student to particular procedures or presupposes results that have not yet been obtained.
Use section headings only when they improve navigation; excessive headings and subdivisions can disrupt the mathematical narrative.
Avoid explicitly labelling sections as demonstrations of personal engagement or reflection.
Make the purpose of each new mathematical process clear before it is carried out.
Explain how one stage of the investigation leads to the next.
Relate each substantial calculation, diagram, table or model to the aim.
Introduce mathematical representations at the point where they are needed rather than placing them in disconnected blocks.
Discuss and interpret results close to where they are obtained, rather than presenting several pages of graphs or calculations before discussing their meaning.
Explain changes in approach when the investigation develops differently from the initial plan.
Remove mathematical processes that are interesting but do not contribute meaningfully to achieving the aim.
Ensure the reader can follow the investigation without repeatedly turning backwards to find essential explanations.
Remove repetitive explanations, redundant calculations and unnecessary commentary.
Show a representative calculation where useful rather than repeating essentially identical calculations for multiple datasets.
Avoid lengthy textbook explanations of standard mathematical concepts already familiar to students on the course.
Remove unnecessary calculator instructions, software procedures and screenshots.
Place extensive raw data and repeated calculations in appendices when they would otherwise interrupt the narrative.
Retain essential mathematics, key data, explanations and reasoning in the main exploration; do not hide material needed for understanding or assessment in an appendix.
Summarise and reference appendix material where it supports the main investigation.
Avoid exceptionally long appendices of data that provide little additional value.
Aim for genuine conciseness rather than simply meeting a particular page count.
Ensure the conclusion clearly addresses the original aim.
Bring together the important mathematical findings rather than simply repeat the sequence of calculations.
Do not introduce new investigations or substantial new evaluations after the conclusion.
Check that the conclusion is consistent with the actual results and any changes made during the investigation.
Define variables and parameters clearly when first introduced.
Define them in the context of the investigation rather than relying only on abstract mathematical descriptions.
Include units where relevant.
Choose meaningful variable symbols, particularly when representing several quantities with different units or meanings.
Use uppercase and lowercase letters consistently; do not interchange them unintentionally.
Italicise variables appropriately in both mathematical expressions and explanatory text.
Use subscripts and superscripts correctly and consistently.
Use an equation editor or another appropriate typesetting method to present conventional mathematical notation.
Replace calculator and computer syntax, such as *, ^ or E, with appropriate standard mathematical notation.
Distinguish clearly between multiplication signs, variable letters and the letter x.
Use mathematical symbols such as χ², Σ, π, r, R², and correctly.
Distinguish accurately between equations, expressions, functions, formulae and mathematical identities.
Use terms such as correlation, causation, proof, significance, independence and accuracy with their correct mathematical meanings.
Use notation for functions and derivatives consistently; for example, avoid unexplained switching between y, f(x) and derivative notation.
Give different model functions distinguishable names or symbols rather than repeatedly using the same undefined function notation.
Ensure mathematical operations and transformations are not merely described in words when they should be shown in mathematical notation.
AA HL: Take care with the notation for more advanced processes, including integration, differential equations and separation of variables.
Give graphs informative titles where appropriate.
Label every graph axis with the quantity represented.
Include units on axes where relevant.
Use appropriate scales and numerical markings for the data and context.
Retain axis labels and scales when zooming into a particular part of a graph.
Use mathematically appropriate domains and ranges, especially for models representing real situations.
Make graph labels, annotations, symbols and plotted data large enough to be read comfortably.
Use appropriate terminology for the particular mathematical representation, including specialised representations such as Voronoi diagrams.
Select diagrams and graph types that genuinely help communicate the investigation.
Do not insert irrelevant charts simply to demonstrate a variety of representations.
Make the meaning and relevance of mathematical figures clear in the surrounding explanation.
Give tables clear headings, including the quantities and units being presented.
Ensure equations, tables and diagrams are not cut off, distorted or rendered incorrectly.
Avoid splitting equations across lines or tables and figures awkwardly across pages.
Keep figure captions, headings and their associated mathematical representations together where practical.
Use = for equality and appropriately for rounded or approximate results.
Apply approximation notation consistently throughout the investigation, rather than only in the final answer.
Choose sensible degrees of accuracy for calculations, measurements and reported results.
Justify rounding or precision decisions in the context of the investigation.
Maintain consistent levels of precision and explain any deliberate changes.
Use appropriate decimal separators and conventional number formatting.
Ensure reported precision does not imply greater accuracy than the underlying data or method supports.
Write for a fellow student studying the same IB Mathematics course.
Explain mathematical concepts, symbols and specialist terminology that would not reasonably be familiar to that audience.
Avoid lengthy explanations of basic mathematics already understood by the intended reader.
Introduce formulae when they are used rather than providing disconnected lists of formulae at the start.
Do not include formulae, variables or representations that have no role in the actual investigation.
Present the mathematical results needed from technology in a clear mathematical format rather than relying on unedited calculator screenshots.
Proofread notation and mathematical formatting as carefully as the written prose.
Demonstrate personal engagement through independent mathematical thinking and decision-making throughout the investigation.
Make it apparent how the student has shaped the investigation rather than simply followed instructions or reproduced an established method.
Use personal interests as a starting point, but develop those interests into substantive mathematical questions.
Avoid relying on a lengthy explanation of personal motivation as evidence of engagement.
Do not assume that effort, time spent, enthusiasm or difficulty of the work demonstrates personal engagement.
Ask original questions that influence which mathematics is investigated.
Make informed choices between possible mathematical approaches and explain the reasons for those choices.
Adapt established mathematical methods to suit the particular problem rather than applying them mechanically.
Investigate different relevant mathematical perspectives when they improve understanding of the problem.
Avoid introducing additional models or methods merely to create the appearance of exploring multiple perspectives.
Make predictions or conjectures and use mathematical evidence to test them.
Investigate unusual cases, extremes, special cases or variations of the original problem where they are relevant.
Consider whether a mathematical finding can be generalised or extended.
Use mathematical results to create new questions and influence the next stage of the investigation.
Refine or modify an approach in response to evidence, rather than following a predetermined sequence regardless of the results.
Where appropriate, design original experiments, investigations or surveys to explore personally meaningful questions.
Explain and justify independent choices involved in the design of those experiments or investigations.
Understand that collecting primary data is neither compulsory nor, by itself, sufficient to demonstrate high personal engagement.
If using primary data, demonstrate how it informed the student's subsequent mathematical decisions.
Recognise that secondary data can still support genuine engagement when used for an independent mathematical investigation.
Where new mathematics is learned, demonstrate that it is understood, relevant and actively used rather than reproduced mechanically.
Personalise familiar investigations through meaningful changes to the problem, assumptions, data or mathematical approach.
Avoid rigid templates, common worked examples or prescribed sequences that leave the student little opportunity to make decisions.
Ensure that the student's own reasoning and mathematical voice remain apparent throughout the work.
Reflect throughout the investigation rather than concentrating reflection in the conclusion.
Review the mathematics after important stages before deciding how to proceed.
Explain the significance of results in relation to the original aim.
Distinguish between stating a result, interpreting it and critically evaluating its mathematical meaning and reliability.
Explain what the results reveal and what they do not establish.
Consider whether a result is mathematically reasonable and plausible in its real-world context.
Identify unexpected findings, contradictions or inconsistencies and investigate their possible causes.
Evaluate the strengths and weaknesses of the mathematical approaches actually used.
Assess whether each chosen method was appropriate for the problem being investigated.
Consider whether a different method would have been more effective or reliable.
Compare approaches where there is a mathematically meaningful basis for comparison.
Allow reflection to change the direction of the investigation when the mathematics suggests a better approach.
Investigate why an attempted method was unsuccessful rather than simply abandoning it.
Use reflective questions to motivate further mathematical investigation.
Identify the assumptions on which mathematical processes, models or conclusions depend.
Explain whether those assumptions are reasonable in the context of the investigation.
Consider how changing an assumption would affect the results.
Investigate the reliability of the mathematical conclusions rather than assuming correct calculations guarantee reliable findings.
Examine how the accuracy of data and measurements affects the conclusions.
Evaluate how rounding, approximation or numerical uncertainty could influence the results or predictions.
Consider the implications of data quality, sample size, sampling bias and representativeness where appropriate.
Analyse the effect of unusual values, outliers or inconsistencies within the data.
Evaluate the limitations of mathematical models, including their suitability for the real situation represented.
Consider whether a model remains valid across the proposed domain.
Where relevant, investigate the sensitivity of results to changes in parameters or inputs.
Discuss the effect of model choice, assumptions and domain restrictions on predictions.
AA HL / modelling: Consider properties such as continuity and smoothness when piecewise mathematical models are used.
Quantify or otherwise demonstrate the effects of important limitations wherever this is possible and meaningful.
Distinguish limitations that materially affect the conclusion from minor or irrelevant imperfections.
Do not simply restate calculations, graph features or numerical findings and label the commentary as reflection.
Avoid generic limitations that could apply to almost any investigation.
Do not suggest collecting more data without considering why the existing data is insufficient and how more data would improve the mathematics.
Avoid offering vague improvements such as using better equipment or more accurate measurements without analysing their likely effects.
Make suggested improvements realistic and relevant to the problem.
Avoid discussing every conceivable limitation when most have no significant relationship to the aim.
Do not substitute personal opinions, general knowledge or observations from another subject for mathematical evaluation.
Do not treat statements about how much the student learned or how difficult the task was as evidence of mathematical reflection.
Avoid a generic limitations-and-extensions section added as an afterthought.
Present reflection in connected analytical prose rather than as an isolated checklist of observations.
Evaluate how successfully the investigation answered its original aim.
Distinguish conclusions supported by the mathematics from speculation.
Explain the significance, validity and scope of the final conclusions.
Identify the most important remaining uncertainties or unresolved mathematical questions.
Where further investigation is suggested, explain how it follows from the findings and what it could establish.
Pure mathematics investigations: Reflect on important mathematical obstacles, choices, proofs and developments even when there is no real-world dataset or mathematical model to evaluate.
Select mathematical processes that genuinely contribute to answering the investigation's aim.
Ensure the mathematics is appropriate for the level of the course.
Use mathematics sufficiently developed beyond simple prior-learning calculations to demonstrate course-level understanding.
Avoid selecting unnecessarily advanced mathematics simply to create an impression of sophistication.
Do not apply a method merely because it is available in the syllabus or because the student knows how to perform it.
Use the simplest appropriate mathematical method when a more complicated approach provides no additional benefit.
Avoid formula-substitution exercises in which the underlying mathematical reasoning is absent.
Maintain the mathematical focus when using concepts from physics, economics, computer science or other disciplines.
Explain why each important mathematical method is suitable for the particular problem.
Demonstrate understanding of the concepts underlying the mathematics rather than relying solely on correct numerical answers.
Explain the meaning and relevance of mathematical results in the context of the investigation.
Interpret parameters, coefficients, constants and other quantities arising from the mathematics.
Explain the mathematical assumptions, requirements and conditions under which a procedure is valid.
Demonstrate understanding of mathematical relationships rather than merely manipulating symbols correctly.
Use mathematical reasoning to explain how a calculation or formula contributes to the investigation.
When introducing mathematics outside the syllabus, provide sufficient explanation for a student on the same course to understand the reasoning.
Where unfamiliar formulae or advanced techniques are essential, explain their mathematical basis rather than simply quoting and applying them.
Avoid lengthy derivations of familiar syllabus formulae when these do not demonstrate additional understanding.
Do not reproduce established derivations or textbook work without meaningful independent mathematical development.
Use clear mathematical explanations, worked examples or appropriate verification to demonstrate the processes have been understood.
Ensure that the reasoning is self-contained, rather than requiring a reader to consult an external source to follow the mathematics.
Use technology efficiently for calculations and processes where it is an appropriate mathematical tool.
Do not assume that performing lengthy calculations manually is automatically better than using technology.
Avoid routine manual calculations of statistical measures when technology can perform them and the calculations add no mathematical insight.
Do not reproduce calculator-generated results without interpreting or explaining their mathematical significance.
Check technology-generated results for plausibility and accuracy rather than accepting them unquestioningly.
Where useful, demonstrate understanding through a representative worked example, independent check or explanation of the underlying mathematical process.
Use programming and simulations to support mathematical thinking rather than allowing the technical implementation to replace mathematical reasoning.
Ensure that the final mathematics demonstrates what the student understands, not simply what the technology can produce.
Identify the population being investigated and define it clearly.
Identify the sampling unit and, where relevant, the sampling frame.
State and explain the sampling technique actually used rather than simply describing a sample as random.
Describe how the sample was obtained in enough detail for the process to be understood.
Justify the choice of sampling technique in relation to the investigation's aim.
Consider whether the sample is representative of the population about which conclusions are being drawn.
Justify the sample size rather than treating any chosen number of observations as automatically sufficient.
Consider the effects of potential selection bias and other weaknesses of the sampling process.
Design questionnaires, experiments and measurement procedures so that the data collected are relevant to the mathematical aim.
Explain important decisions about survey questions, measurement procedures, variables and data collection.
Verify that the data source is credible and sufficiently reliable for the intended analysis.
Distinguish between different types of data when determining which mathematical techniques are appropriate.
Consider measurement uncertainty, incomplete observations and potential sources of error.
Evaluate whether the collected data are suitable for the proposed statistical or modelling methods.
Consider the limitations of secondary datasets rather than accepting their reliability automatically.
Distinguish between genuine anomalous observations and errors in data collection or recording.
Justify decisions to exclude, modify or retain individual data values.
When investigating relationships between two variables, assess possible outliers in the paired data rather than removing observations solely because they appear unusual in one variable.
Consider how the data collection method might affect the reliability and generalisability of the eventual conclusions.
Present enough of the original data for the reader to understand how the analysis relates to the evidence.
Plot the data and examine its distribution before calculating correlation coefficients or fitting a regression model.
Initially examine a scatterplot without automatically adding a regression line, so that the underlying trend can be investigated.
Consider the shape, spread, clustering and possible outliers in bivariate data.
Justify the use of Pearson's or Spearman's correlation coefficient according to the nature of the data and investigation.
Explain the meaning of the calculated correlation coefficient in the context of the actual variables.
Distinguish between the strength and direction of an association and the existence of a causal relationship.
Do not interpret correlation as proof that one variable causes changes in another.
Do not interpret statistical independence or dependence automatically as evidence of influence or causation.
Consider whether the data provide sufficient evidence of a relationship before attempting to model that relationship.
Avoid calculating a linear regression equation when the data show little justification for a linear relationship.
Where linear correlation is weak or absent, consider whether other variables, relationships or appropriate nonlinear models warrant investigation.
Do not assume that a higher correlation or goodness-of-fit statistic automatically produces a mathematically better explanation.
Explain the meaning of statistical measures such as r, r² and R², using their symbols and interpretations correctly.
Choose a statistical test because it addresses a specific question arising from the aim, not simply because it appears in the syllabus.
Explain why the selected statistical test is appropriate for the type and structure of data.
Identify the assumptions and conditions required for the statistical test to be valid.
Verify that these conditions are satisfied or discuss the consequences where they are not.
Distinguish clearly between the purposes of a chi-squared test for independence and a chi-squared goodness-of-fit test.
Explain the conditions and requirements of other tests used, including t-tests and, where undertaken, ANOVA.
State the null and alternative hypotheses accurately and in the context of the investigation.
Use the conventional mathematical notation and structure required for the chosen test.
Establish and justify the significance level before examining the result of the test.
Present the appropriate test statistic and p-value, where applicable, with meaningful interpretation.
Explain the conclusion of the test in relation to the original aim and the data.
Avoid overstating what a statistically significant or non-significant result establishes.
Do not perform a sequence of unrelated statistical tests merely to increase the amount of mathematics displayed.
Ensure that univariate descriptive statistics are included only when they help answer the question being investigated or inform subsequent analysis.
Present both the observed and expected frequency information needed to understand and evaluate the test.
Check the expected frequencies and degrees of freedom before relying on the test results.
Recognise that small expected frequencies require consideration of the validity of the procedure.
Consider whether regrouping categories is appropriate when expected frequencies are too small.
When continuous data are grouped into categories, justify the choice of class intervals or bin widths.
Investigate whether continuity corrections, including Yates' correction where relevant, are appropriate rather than applying them mechanically.
Do not assume that a test remains reliable when its conditions are violated simply because technology produces a result.
Recognise that performing a chi-squared test after finding weak correlation does not automatically provide a meaningful continuation of the investigation.
Examine and describe the behaviour of the data before choosing a model.
Identify important features such as trends, turning points, rates of change, possible asymptotes and limiting behaviour where relevant.
Choose candidate functions whose mathematical properties are appropriate for the phenomenon being modelled.
Justify the choice of function using mathematical and contextual reasoning rather than simply comparing software outputs.
Do not select models randomly or use trial and error without explaining why the candidate functions are appropriate.
Avoid automatically selecting high-degree polynomial models because they achieve a particularly high coefficient of determination.
Where parameters are calculated algebraically, justify the selection of coordinates or conditions used to determine them.
Recognise that using regression technology to estimate model parameters can be more appropriate than arbitrarily selecting a few points and solving simultaneous equations.
Explain the significance of model parameters and how they relate to the real situation.
Consider whether the model's mathematical characteristics agree with what is known about the phenomenon.
Evaluate how well the model fits the observed data rather than assuming a successful calculation establishes a good model.
Consider the distribution of the data around the fitted function.
Use relevant graphical or numerical evidence to compare model quality.
Where appropriate, examine residuals or other evidence of systematic differences between the model and the data.
Do not rely exclusively on R² when selecting or validating a model.
Distinguish between fitting a model within the observed data range and using it to make predictions beyond that range.
Treat interpolation and extrapolation differently when evaluating the usefulness of a model.
Consider whether the function behaves reasonably outside the original dataset before using it for prediction.
Establish meaningful domain and range restrictions based on the context.
Investigate whether predictions generated by the model are realistic.
Where appropriate, compare predictions with observations or other mathematical evidence.
Evaluate the effects of outliers, rounding and parameter choices on the resulting model.
Refine the model when its limitations or mathematical behaviour suggest improvements are necessary.
When combining functions into a piecewise model, consider whether the sections meet appropriately and whether continuity or smoothness is required.
Explain why a final model is suitable for the particular aim rather than merely declaring it the best-fitting function.

Voronoi diagrams (particularly AI SL): Demonstrate understanding of the geometric properties, construction and purpose of the diagram rather than simply following the algorithm or using software to generate it.
Voronoi applications: Explain how the resulting regions, boundaries or spatial relationships support conclusions about the real-world situation being investigated.
Optimization and calculus: Ensure the mathematical work genuinely investigates an optimization or modelling problem rather than reproducing a standard textbook example with different numbers.
Pure mathematics: Develop and investigate the mathematical ideas rather than merely present the history of a concept or reproduce an established proof.
Probability and games: Explain the necessary rules, assumptions, outcomes and mathematical structure so that the investigation is comprehensible to someone unfamiliar with the game.
Game-based investigations: Avoid allowing descriptions of game mechanics or background information to overwhelm the mathematical work.
Simulations: Where simulations are used, explain their mathematical meaning and the connection between simulated results, mathematical assumptions and conclusions.
Introduce the nature and purpose of the mathematical exploration early in the course.
Integrate exploration-style activities throughout the mathematics curriculum rather than treating the IA as an isolated final task.
Highlight potential IA investigations as different mathematical topics are taught.
Provide students with experience of shorter mathematical investigations or mini-IAs.
Use these shorter investigations to practise formulating aims, choosing mathematics, communicating reasoning, interpreting results and reflecting.
Make explicit connections between routine curriculum mathematics and possible investigative applications.
Use the mathematical toolkit and technology activities to develop the skills students will later need for their explorations.
Teach students how to use equation editors, graphing technology, spreadsheets and other mathematical software effectively.
Provide opportunities to practise selecting appropriate graphs, scales, labels, notation and units.
Teach correct mathematical terminology and provide suitable reference materials where useful.
Teach statistical techniques alongside their conditions, assumptions and appropriate applications, not merely as procedures to execute.
Give students regular opportunities to justify mathematical choices and explain the meaning of results.
Explicitly model the difference between descriptive comments, mathematical interpretation, meaningful reflection and critical reflection.
Use mathematical exercises in which students evaluate methods, identify weaknesses, examine assumptions and propose justified improvements.
Provide practice with mathematical writing and extended investigative explanations, including where technology is used to complete calculations.
Ensure students understand all five IA criteria before they begin drafting.
Revisit the criteria during the investigation process rather than only when the work is marked.
Give particular attention to Criteria C, D and E, which examiners repeatedly identify as difficult or misunderstood.
Use the official Teacher Support Material and annotated exemplar explorations to demonstrate the standards expected.
Provide students with examples from different mathematical pathways and types of investigation.
Let students practise marking exemplar explorations using the official criteria.
Compare their judgements with the available marked exemplars and moderated commentary.
Use collaborative discussions to identify why different explorations achieve particular criterion levels.
Show students the common weaknesses highlighted in previous subject reports and discuss how they can be avoided.
Support students in generating and evaluating possible investigation ideas.
Review proposals early enough to identify unsuitable, unmanageable or mathematically weak topics.
Guide students away from topics that provide too little mathematical opportunity or require mathematics far beyond their understanding.
Ensure students are not encouraged to select advanced mathematics simply because it appears impressive.
Avoid directing all students towards the same statistical methodology or investigation template.
Preserve students' independence and ownership of the topic and mathematical decisions.
Allow topics to develop as the course progresses rather than requiring final mathematical choices too early.
Time the formal development of the exploration so that students have encountered sufficient relevant course mathematics.
Provide clear progress checkpoints and sufficient time for students to develop, evaluate and revise their thinking.
Continue to support students after their topic proposals have been accepted.
Encourage students to seek advice when they encounter mathematical problems or difficulties.
Provide appropriate feedback on the permitted draft, identifying problems and areas for improvement without rewriting or correcting the exploration for the student.
Encourage peer review where permitted, particularly for mathematical clarity, notation and readability.
Ensure peer feedback identifies possible errors or confusing passages without supplying replacement solutions.
Monitor student progress to avoid rushed, incomplete or formulaic submissions.
Read the relevant IB subject guide, Teacher Support Material and recent subject reports before assessing explorations.
Use the correct assessment criteria for the course and examination session rather than criteria from previous mathematics courses.
Apply the descriptors according to the mathematical evidence present in the submitted work.
Avoid awarding high marks simply because an exploration is well written, visually polished or mathematically complicated.
Assess personal engagement on the evidence of mathematical ownership rather than effort, enthusiasm or topic choice.
Distinguish meaningful mathematical reflection from descriptive commentary when assessing Criterion D.
Assess mathematical understanding rather than the number, length or apparent difficulty of calculations.
Avoid over-generous marking, particularly in Criteria C, D and E.
Use officially marked exemplars to calibrate judgements about achievement levels.
Ensure that the awarded marks are consistent with the strengths and weaknesses actually identified in the exploration.
Check the mathematical accuracy of student calculations and reasoning rather than assuming that the work is correct.
Clearly indicate where mathematical errors occur.
Mark correct mathematical working appropriately; do not place ticks beside incorrect mathematics.
Annotate the actual student exploration to identify evidence relevant to the assessment criteria.
Make annotations specific to the student's work rather than merely quoting or paraphrasing criterion descriptors.
Identify both positive evidence and weaknesses that explain the awarded levels.
Make clear where and how particular achievement descriptors have been met.
Provide criterion-specific comments that justify the assessment decisions.
Where separate commentary is used, refer precisely to the relevant evidence in the student exploration.
Avoid submitting entirely unannotated scripts accompanied only by brief general comments.
Avoid relying on occasional ticks, criterion letters or generic positive statements as the sole assessment commentary.
Ensure annotations are legible and do not obscure the student's mathematics.
Avoid separate numbered comment lists that require moderators to move repeatedly between the commentary and student work.
Where relevant, provide helpful context about mathematics covered during the course or material the student independently studied.
Conduct internal standardisation when more than one teacher assesses Mathematics IAs.
Use the same official assessment criteria and interpretation across the department.
Compare teacher judgements using common exemplar explorations and moderation commentary.
Discuss discrepancies in the assessment of mathematical understanding, personal engagement and reflection.
Review individual assessment decisions where the annotations do not justify the marks awarded.
Ensure that the final comments and marks correspond to the actual submitted student work.
Use moderation outcomes and previous examiner feedback to improve departmental assessment practices.
Cite external sources at the point where their information, ideas, mathematical methods or other material is used.
Ensure each in-text citation corresponds to an appropriate bibliography entry.
Include only sources that were actually used in developing the investigation.
Do not pad the bibliography with sources that did not inform the work.
Understand that a bibliography is not necessarily required when no external sources have been used, but appropriate referencing is essential whenever external material is incorporated.
Cite externally obtained diagrams, images, mathematical expressions, models and other reproduced material.
Distinguish the student's own mathematical reasoning from mathematics, results or explanations obtained from external sources.
Avoid copying or closely paraphrasing substantial passages of textbook or online mathematics and presenting them as independent mathematical exploration.
Ensure that the mathematical reasoning can be understood within the submitted IA rather than depending on linked resources or external explanations.
Check that references are accurate and genuinely support the claims or mathematical work for which they are cited.
Acknowledge and reference the use of AI tools where required by IB academic integrity expectations.
Explain the nature of AI assistance where appropriate rather than leaving its contribution unclear.
Ensure that the student's own mathematical understanding and reasoning remain demonstrable.
Avoid formulaic, AI-generated introductions or generic reflective writing that does not represent genuine student thinking.
Verify mathematical statements, formulae and reasoning obtained from AI or other external sources.
Do not allow polished language to conceal weak mathematical understanding.
Maintain sufficient teacher supervision and developmental evidence to establish the authenticity of the exploration.
Avoid providing identical investigation structures or mathematical procedures to an entire class in ways that undermine independence or increase academic integrity concerns.
Review student work and source use carefully before confirming its authenticity for submission.
Use a clear title that accurately identifies the investigation.
Include the required page count and page numbering.
Use professional, consistent formatting, spacing and margins.
Avoid manipulating font size, spacing or layout merely to make the work appear shorter or longer.
Treat the historically suggested 12-20-page length as guidance rather than a guarantee of conciseness or quality.

Follow the formatting requirements in the subject guide applicable to the examination session. The older reports contain differing font-size recommendations and refer to double spacing, so these should not be treated as a substitute for checking the applicable guide.
Proofread the complete document for mathematical and typographical errors.
Check that diagrams, equations and tables are correctly positioned and remain readable.
Ensure all necessary information is included in the document rather than relying on QR codes or external hyperlinks.

Remove identifying information, including student names, candidate numbers, teacher names and school names, from submitted documentation.
Check anonymisation on the student exploration, accompanying teacher comments and marking documentation.
Preserve colour in uploaded scans where colour is needed to interpret the mathematical work.
Ensure graphs and mathematical figures remain interpretable in the form submitted to moderators.
Check that mathematical symbols, equations and expressions have not disappeared or changed during PDF conversion.
